replacement: Now it is an unquestionable fact that people who know both kinds of pleasure equally well, and are equally able to appreciate and enjoy both, markedly prefer the way of life that engages their higher faculties. Few human creatures would accept being turned into one of the lower animals, even for a promise of the fullest share of a beast's pleasures. No intelligent person would agree to be a fool, no instructed person an ignoramus, no person of feeling and conscience selfish and base, even if convinced that the fool, the dunce, or the rascal is better satisfied with his lot than they are with theirs. They would not trade away what they have beyond what he has, not even for the complete satisfaction of every desire they share with him. If they ever imagine they would, it is only in a state of unhappiness so extreme that they would swap their lot for almost any other to escape it, however undesirable they found that other lot. A being with higher faculties needs more in order to be happy, is probably able to suffer more acutely, and is certainly exposed to suffering at more points than a being of an inferior type. Despite all this, he can never truly wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence. We may explain this unwillingness however we like. We may put it down to pride, a name that gets applied without distinction to some of the most and some of the least estimable feelings mankind has. We may trace it to the love of liberty and personal independence, which the Stoics appealed to as one of the most effective ways of teaching it; or to the love of power, or to the love of excitement, both of which really do play a part in it. But the name that fits it best is a sense of dignity. Every human being has this in one form or another, and in some it matches their higher faculties, though by no means exactly. For those in whom it is strong, it is so essential a part of their happiness that nothing in conflict with it could attract them, except for a moment. Anyone who supposes that this preference costs the superior being some happiness — that he is not happier than the inferior one in anything like equal circumstances — is confounding two very different ideas, happiness and content. It is indisputable that a being with low capacities for enjoyment has the best chance of satisfying them fully, while a highly endowed being will always feel that whatever happiness he can look for, in the world as it is, is imperfect. But he can learn to put up with its imperfections, if they are at all bearable. And they will not make him envy the being who is unconscious of them, since that being is unconscious only because he does not feel at all the good which those imperfections qualify. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question. The other party to the comparison knows both sides.

[Footnote B: An opponent, whose intellectual and moral fairness it is a pleasure to acknowledge (the Rev. J. Llewellyn Davis), has objected to this passage. He says, "Surely the rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much upon the motive with which it is done. Suppose that a tyrant, when his enemy jumped into the sea to escape from him, saved him from drowning simply in order that he might inflict upon him more exquisite tortures, would it tend to clearness to speak of that rescue as 'a morally right action?' Or suppose again, according to one of the stock illustrations of ethical inquiries, that a man betrayed a trust received from a friend, because the discharge of it would fatally injure that friend himself or some one belonging to him, would utilitarianism compel one to call the betrayal 'a crime' as much as if it had been done from the meanest motive?" I submit that the man who saves another from drowning in order to kill him by torture afterward does not differ from the man who does the same thing from duty or benevolence in motive only. The act itself is different. In the case supposed, the rescue is only the necessary first step of an act far more atrocious than leaving him to drown would have been. Suppose Mr. Davis had said, "The rightness or wrongness of saving a man from drowning does depend very much" — not upon the motive, but — "upon the _intention_." No utilitarian would have differed from him. Through an oversight too common not to be quite venial, Mr. Davis has in this case confounded the very different ideas of Motive and Intention. There is no point that utilitarian thinkers (and Bentham pre-eminently) have taken more pains to illustrate. The morality of the action depends entirely on the intention, that is, on what the agent _wills to do_. But the motive, that is, the feeling that makes him will so to do, makes no difference in the morality when it makes none in the act. It does make a great difference in our moral estimation of the agent, especially if it indicates a good or a bad habitual _disposition_, a bent of character from which useful actions, or hurtful ones, are likely to arise.]

The principle of utility has all the sanctions that belong to any other system of morals, or at least there is no reason why it might not have them. Those sanctions are either external or internal. I need not speak at any length of the external sanctions. They are the hope of favor and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe. Along with these go whatever sympathy or affection we may have for our fellow creatures, or love and awe of Him, which incline us to do His will independently of selfish consequences. There is plainly no reason why all these motives for observance should not attach themselves to the utilitarian morality as completely and as powerfully as to any other. Indeed, those that concern our fellow creatures are sure to do so in proportion to the amount of general intelligence. For whether or not there is any other ground of moral obligation than the general happiness, men do desire happiness. However imperfect their own practice may be, they desire and commend all conduct in others toward themselves by which they think their happiness is promoted. As for the religious motive, if men believe in the goodness of God, as most profess to do, then those who think that conduciveness to the general happiness is the essence of good, or even only its criterion, must necessarily believe that it is also what God approves. So the whole force of external reward and punishment, whether physical or moral, and whether it comes from God or from our fellow men, becomes available to enforce the utilitarian morality, in proportion as that morality is recognized. The same holds for all the disinterested devotion to either that human nature admits of. And the more education and general cultivation are bent to this purpose, the more powerful that force becomes.

But does the utilitarian doctrine deny that people desire virtue? Does it maintain that virtue is not a thing to be desired? The very reverse. It maintains that virtue is to be desired, and desired disinterestedly, for itself. Utilitarian moralists may hold any opinion about the original conditions that make virtue what it is. They may believe (as they do) that actions and dispositions are virtuous only because they promote some end other than virtue. Yet once this is granted, and once such considerations have settled what _is_ virtuous, they do two things. First, they put virtue at the very head of the things that are good as means to the ultimate end. Second, they recognize as a psychological fact that virtue may be, for the individual, a good in itself, with no looking to any end beyond it. They hold that the mind is not in a right state, not in a state conformable to Utility, not in the state most conducive to the general happiness, unless it loves virtue in this manner, as a thing desirable in itself. This holds even if, in the individual instance, virtue does not produce the other desirable consequences it tends to produce, and on account of which it is held to be virtue. This opinion is not in the smallest degree a departure from the Happiness principle. Happiness has very various ingredients, and each of them is desirable in itself, not merely when counted as swelling an aggregate. The principle of utility does not mean that a given pleasure, such as music, or a given exemption from pain, such as health, should be looked on as a means to some collective something called happiness, and desired on that account. They are desired and desirable in and for themselves. Besides being means, they are a part of the end. On the utilitarian doctrine, virtue is not naturally and originally part of the end, but it is capable of becoming so. In those who love it disinterestedly it has become so. They desire and cherish it not as a means to happiness but as a part of their happiness.

With this moral sentiment, as with our others, the question of its origin is not necessarily connected with the question of its binding force. That Nature has given us a feeling does not by itself justify everything the feeling urges. The feeling of justice might be a peculiar instinct and yet need, like our other instincts, to be controlled and enlightened by a higher reason. We have intellectual instincts, which lead us to judge in a particular way, as well as animal instincts, which prompt us to act in a particular way. There is no necessity that the former be more infallible in their sphere than the latter in theirs. Wrong judgments may occasionally be suggested by the one just as wrong actions are by the other. But it is one thing to believe that we have natural feelings of justice, and another to accept them as an ultimate criterion of conduct. Even so, in point of fact, these two opinions are very closely connected. Mankind are always predisposed to believe that any subjective feeling which cannot be accounted for in some other way is a revelation of some objective reality. Our present object is to determine whether the reality to which the feeling of justice corresponds is one that needs any such special revelation. Is the justice or injustice of an action something intrinsically peculiar, distinct from all its other qualities? Or is it only a combination of certain of those qualities, seen under a peculiar aspect? For this inquiry it is practically important to ask whether the feeling of justice and injustice is itself _sui generis_, like our sensations of color and taste, or is a derivative feeling, formed by a combination of others. It is all the more essential to examine this because people are in general willing enough to allow that, objectively, the dictates of justice coincide with a part of the field of General Expediency. But the subjective mental feeling of Justice differs from the feeling that commonly attaches to simple expediency, and, except in extreme cases of the latter, it is far more imperative in its demands. So people find it difficult to see in Justice only a particular kind or branch of general utility, and they think that its superior binding force requires a totally different origin.

Closely allied to impartiality is the idea of _equality_. It often enters as a component into both the conception and the practice of justice, and many people see it as the essence of justice. But here, even more than elsewhere, different people hold different notions of justice, and the variations always follow their notion of utility. Each person holds that equality is what justice dictates, unless he thinks expediency calls for inequality. Even the defenders of the most outrageous inequality in the rights themselves maintain that the rights of all deserve equal protection. Even in slave countries it is admitted in theory that the slave's rights, such as they are, ought to be as sacred as the master's, and that a tribunal which enforces them less strictly is lacking in justice. Yet institutions that leave the slave hardly any rights to enforce are not deemed unjust, because they are not deemed inexpedient. People who think utility requires distinctions of rank see no injustice in an unequal distribution of riches and social privileges. People who think that inequality inexpedient think it unjust too. Whoever thinks government necessary sees no injustice in the inequality created when a magistrate is given powers that other people lack. Even among the holders of levelling doctrines there are as many questions of justice as there are differences of opinion about expediency. Some Communists consider it unjust to share the produce of the community's labor on any principle but exact equality. Others think it just that those with the greatest needs receive most. Others hold that those who work harder, or produce more, or give more valuable service to the community, may justly claim a larger share of the produce. And the sense of natural justice can plausibly be called on in support of every one of these opinions.

It is no objection to this doctrine to say that when we feel our sentiment of justice outraged, we are not thinking of society at large, or of any collective interest, but only of the individual case. It is common enough, certainly, though the reverse of commendable, to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain. But consider a person whose resentment is really a moral feeling, that is, who considers whether an act is blameable before he allows himself to resent it. Such a person may not say expressly to himself that he is standing up for the interest of society, but he certainly does feel that he is asserting a rule which is for the benefit of others as well as for his own. If he is not feeling this, and is regarding the act solely as it affects him individually, he is not consciously just: he is not concerning himself about the justice of his actions. Even anti-utilitarian moralists admit this. When Kant (as remarked before) propounds as the fundamental principle of morals, "So act, that thy rule of conduct might be adopted as a law by all rational beings," he virtually acknowledges that the interest of mankind collectively, or at least of mankind indiscriminately, must be in the mind of the agent when he is conscientiously deciding on the morality of the act. Otherwise he uses words without a meaning. For it cannot even be plausibly maintained that even a rule of utter selfishness could not _possibly_ be adopted by all rational beings, or that there is any insuperable obstacle in the nature of things to its adoption. To give any meaning to Kant's principle, the sense put on it must be that we ought to shape our conduct by a rule which all rational beings might adopt _with benefit to their collective interest_.

To have a right, then, is, I hold, to have something that society ought to defend me in possessing. Suppose the objector goes on to ask why society ought to do so. I can give him no reason but general utility. Suppose that expression does not seem to convey enough of the strength of the obligation, or to explain the peculiar energy of the feeling. If so, the cause is that the sentiment is composed of an animal element, the thirst for retaliation, as well as a rational one. That thirst draws its intensity, and its moral justification, from the extraordinarily important and impressive kind of utility at stake. The interest concerned is security, which everyone feels to be the most vital of all interests. Almost every other earthly benefit is needed by one person and not by another, and many can, if necessary, be cheerfully done without, or replaced by something else. Security, however, no human being can possibly do without. All our immunity from evil depends on it, as does the whole value of every good beyond the passing moment. For if whoever was momentarily stronger than we are could take everything from us the next instant, nothing but the gratification of the instant would be worth anything to us. Now this most indispensable of all necessaries, after physical nutriment, cannot be had unless the machinery that provides it is kept constantly at work. So we claim that our fellow creatures must join in making the very groundwork of our existence safe for us. Feelings gather around this claim that are far more intense than those in any of the more common cases of utility, and so the difference in degree (as often happens in psychology) becomes a real difference in kind. The claim acquires that character of absoluteness, that apparent infinity, that incommensurability with every other consideration, which marks the difference between the feeling of right and wrong and the feeling of ordinary expediency and inexpediency. These feelings are so powerful, and we count so positively on a responsive feeling in others (since all are alike interested), that _ought_ and _should_ grow into _must_. Recognized indispensability becomes a moral necessity, like a physical one, and often equal to it in binding force.
